title: You Can't Actually Be Close to Fifteen People
author: Scott D. Clary
summary: Scott Clary builds on Robin Dunbar's decades of primate research demonstrating that human social capacity operates within fixed biological constraints: approximately 150 casual relationships, 50 decent friendships, 15 close friends, and just 5 intimate bonds. This isn't a matter of personal preference or networking prowess—it's a hard neurological ceiling rooted in how human brains process social information and maintain relationships. The practical implication is a profound shift in mindset around age 30: before that threshold, most people collect friends; after 30, successful people deliberately curate relationships, consciously trading quantitative breadth for qualitative depth. This biological reality forces a trade-off many discover painfully through trial and error.
points: Robin Dunbar's primate research across decades identified a fixed biological hierarchy: humans maintain approximately 150 casual acquaintances, 50 decent friendships, 15 close friends, and only 5 intimate bonds; this cap reflects neurological constraints, not personal failing.

The numbers aren't aspirational or variable—they represent a biological ceiling determined by brain architecture; attempting to maintain more relationships at each tier simply dilutes the quality and presence available for each.

Social strategy shifts decisively around age 30: before this inflection, people generally accumulate friendships; after 30, high-performers transition to deliberate curation, consciously choosing depth over breadth.

Most people discover this constraint through expensive trial and error—burnout, fractured friendships, or shallow networks—rather than proactively designing their social lives around biological reality.

Accepting the constraint enables a deliberate trade: smaller rooms and fewer dinner invitations, but substantially better conversations, deeper understanding, and more genuine presence with those who matter most.
quotes: Before 30, you collect friends. After 30, you curate them. Smaller rooms. Better conversations. That's the trade.

Robin Dunbar spent decades studying primate social groups and discovered something uncomfortable: humans can maintain roughly 150 casual relationships, 50 decent friendships, 15 close friends, and 5 intimate bonds. That's it.
Biology puts a hard cap on how many people you can actually know.” Archived from Scott Clary Newsletter on April 20, 2026 by Tim.
